items.title: Samsung settles four-year Wireless PowerShare patent lawsuit
items.snippet: Samsung has settled a US patent infringement lawsuit over the Wireless PowerShare feature on its Galaxy phones. The company, wireless charging chip supplier Renesas Electronics America, and WiPQTUS recently submitted a joint agreement, withdrawing all claims as part of an out-of-court settlement. Wireless PowerShare lets you charge compatible Galaxy Watches, Galaxy Buds, other Galaxy phones, and Qi-compatible devices by placing them on the back of your handset. The feature first showed up on the Galaxy S10 in 2019, and the complaint also named phones from the Galaxy S20, S21, and S22...

items.snippet: The ongoing Microsoft 365 outage is resolving after nearly 24 hours. The company said the underlying issue has been fixed and it is seeing "broad recovery and stability" across its services as it works to restore access to customers. The Microsoft 365 downtime started at approximately 1 p.m. Eastern Time on Thursday. Customers could not access their Outlook email or use some features in Teams and Copilot. Exchange accounts in Apple Mail were also affected. Most calling, meeting, and messaging functions stayed online, but some users ran into errors scheduling meetings or adding calendar entries. items.title: iPhone Duo Survives 450,000 Folds, but Hinge is Weakening
items.snippet: For the last three weeks, CNET has been stress testing the iPhone Duo 's hinge on a livestream. After over 451,000 folds, the hinge is showing signs of wear. CNET says the hinge started feeling looser at the 390,000-fold point, and by 440,300 folds, there was enough of a shift in the mechanism that the screen didn't open in full before the machine closed it again, and there was no distinctive snap. It is 5 to 10 degrees from the fully open state and can be opened fully by hand. The wire we use to open the phone screen would withdraw before the screen was in the fully open position, but it would then sort of "coast" the rest of the way down. items.snippet: Ryan Mac, Tripp Mickle, and Georgia Gee, reporting for The New York Times: Jensen Huang, the leader of Nvidia who is under investigation for an affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy, also had an extramarital relationship with an executive who reports to him, according to five people who worked at the company. The relationship, which has not been previously reported, was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, said the people, who spoke under the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive information. items.title: Apple Shutters Their Longstanding ‘Apple Support Community’
items.snippet: Jason Snell: These message boards were an embarrassment for Apple. Not only were they very much out of step with what the web has come to be over the last couple of decades, but their presence under an apple.com domain meant that they ranked highly in search and were perceived by the general public as being official in some way. I’m with Snell. Good riddance. ★

items.title: Austin Mann’s iPhone Duo Review
items.snippet: Austin Mann: Honestly, the idea of a folding iPhone didn’t immediately appeal to me. I usually like smaller devices, but when I first started playing with the Duo in September, I realized it’s really something special and I couldn’t wait to get my hands on a review unit from Apple. The iPhone 18 Pro remains the most powerful camera in the lineup, and though the Duo also has an excellent camera, where it really shines is everything around the photograph: planning, editing and sharing. There are many reasons to prefer any of the regular (“uno”) iPhones to the Duo, but for almost everyone, the camera is not one of them. items.title: NTLM signing enforcement in Windows
items.snippet: Microsoft's November 10, 2026, security releases rework how NTLM message signing is negotiated to close CVE-2026-118737 and limit NTLM relay risk. Windows clients now propose actual NTLM signing on every non-anonymous session, whereas servers still allow unsigned clients through. From May 2027 onward, Windows servers will insist on NTLM signing by default and refuse peers that never offer it. This piece covers what changed, the registry DWORDs ClientAllowUnsignedNtlm and ServerRequireNtlmSign , and how audit events 4022 and 4023 help you locate unsigned NTLM before the server-side requirement kicks in. items.title: AMD takes on Intel and Nvidia with new 256-core EPYC server CPUs
